questions.question: What does the browser combine to build the Render Tree?
options: The DOM and the CSSOM, excluding nodes that are not visible (e.g. display: none)
JavaScript's call stack and the DOM
questions.explanation: The Render Tree merges the DOM's structure with the CSSOM's computed styles, keeping only the nodes that will actually be rendered.

questions.question: Why is a stylesheet in `<head>` render-blocking by default, and why is that usually the right trade-off?
options: It's a bug browsers haven't fixed yet
The browser needs the complete CSSOM before painting; blocking avoids painting unstyled content and then jarringly re-painting once styles arrive
Render-blocking CSS makes pages load faster overall
It only blocks images, not text
questions.explanation: Painting before CSS is ready would cause a visible flash of unstyled content, which is normally worse than a brief delay before the styled page appears.

questions.question: Which of these changes triggers a reflow (layout recalculation)?
questions.explanation: Any property that can affect an element's size or position — like width — forces the browser to recompute layout, which is the most expensive of the three rendering stages.

questions.question: Why do `transform` and `opacity` only trigger composite, skipping layout and paint entirely?
options: They are special-cased to be ignored by the rendering pipeline
They can be applied by the GPU directly to an already-painted layer, without needing to recompute geometry or redraw pixels
Modern browsers disable layout entirely for all CSS
questions.explanation: Because transform and opacity don't affect element geometry or require redrawing pixel content, the browser can let the GPU recombine existing painted layers, the cheapest of the three rendering stages.
